items.title: Should boomers give away their inheritance early?
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>As the price of everything rises, millennials are looking to their parents for help. Although a majority of parents in America help their children financially in some capacity, there is a contingent of boomers who insist their children pull themselves up by their bootstraps. 

Charlotte Cowles, a financial columnist for The Cut, spoke to some of these millennials and their boomer parents about why the kids want the money now and why their parents want to wait. She told Vox’s Today, Explained podcast that the assumptions about money made by both the parents and children are stopping families from having much-needed conversations about finances.

https://github.blog/developer-skills/programming-languages-and-frameworks/typescripts-rise-in-the-ai-era-insights-from-lead-architect-anders-hejlsberg

ABSTRACT
Programming languages are a halfway house between the metal and the mind, a bridge between the world of circuits and the world of applications, the engineered and the social. Programming languages are the medium through which developers codify systems and fragments. In each programming language is embedded a philosophy (or many) of how to think about code, how to organise thoughts, how to design. Programming languages also define skillsets, ecosystems, jobs, loyalties and communities.

When we think of software and technology we often think in terms of progress and rapid change. Programming languages, however, typically move at a far slower pace. Mainstream languages are still embracing ideas that are decades old. Constructs that developers welcome as new to their language of choice are often older than the developers themselves.
And over all this hangs the question, what of the future?
How will current trends, from FOSS to LLMs, shape programming languages and their use?

In this talk, we will take a tour of the past, present and future of programming languages. [...]

items.title: We Need To Talk About Leopold
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Taking care of your health just got easier, thanks to my sponsor Zocdoc! Start here at: https://zocdoc.com/patrickboyle

Last week, 24-year-old Leopold Aschenbrenner — former FTX staffer, ex-OpenAI researcher, and author of the viral 165-page essay "Situational Awareness" — managed to lose roughly two-thirds of his $45 billion hedge fund in a matter of weeks. The margin calls arrived during his wedding weekend.

In this video I break down how a trader with no professional experience raised billions from Silicon Valley, why his AI "hedge" wasn't a hedge at all, and how leverage plus a concentrated bet on artificial intelligence stocks turned a great-looking expected return into a catastrophic outcome. Along the way we look at the cultural gap between Silicon Valley and Wall Street, why Ken Griffin's Citadel ended up buying the collapsing portfolio in an overnight fire sale, and the maths of volatility drag — the reason a high expected return can still drag an investor's typical outcome straight into the ground.

It's a story about leverage, risk management, expected versus median returns, and what happens when you go "full Kelly." Featuring reporting from the Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and the Financial Times, plus Victor Haghani's lessons from The Missing Billionaires.

items.title: BookTok and Gen Z - Are young people saving the book market? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The digital book club BookTok got its start during the pandemic in 2020. Today, it is a big success, used primarily by young women who are fans of a particular literary genre - so-called "New Adult,” or romance novels for young adults.

The new books have striking, glossy covers, their language is easy to follow, the stories are romantic, exciting and full of eroticism from a female perspective. But young women aren't just engaging in online discussions about their favorite books. Book blogger Jess 'miss.Nerdstagram' also meets her followers in person at events like the Book Ball at Namedy Castle in Germany.
Author Kim Leopold from the German town of Rheine also frequently takes to the road to be close to her fans. She's an 'own voice' author writing about her own personal experience, in stories that satisfy the hunger for authentic narratives. Topics such as mental health, body positivity and ADHD are close to her heart. Kim is nervously awaiting the release of her latest book, which ventures into new territory: the focus is no longer on a single woman, but on a young married couple. Will this story also resonate with her fans? 
The Riekes are living their dream in Jever: right in the center of town, they've opened a shop dedicated to the New Adult phenomenon. The young entrepreneurs are also a couple in their private lives and post clips on social media as a comedy duo. For them, just as for Kim and Jess, attending the Frankfurt Book Fair is the highlight of the year. But traditional critics at events like these are generally skeptical of these modern literary formats, no matter how vibrant they may be. Can the couple hold their own?

items.title: Bosnia's hidden landmines | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>In early 2026, Finland officially left the Ottawa Treaty, allowing it to buy and stockpile landmines again – a move criticized by human rights groups. Poland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have also exited the treaty, citing security concerns over neighboring Russia. 

First adopted in 1997, the Ottawa Treaty bans the production, stockpiling and use of anti-personnel landmines. More than 160 countries are party to the agreement. 

During the Bosnian War (1992-1995), hundreds of thousands of landmines were scattered across the country. Since the end of the war, more than 1,700 people have been victims of landmines in Bosnia, 600 of whom died. 

Mine-detection dogs are one way to help clear mines, making the land safe for local communities to use again.

items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>Mount Kologet, Goldsboro, Palomares, Thule… Four nuclear accidents, four stains on the history of the Cold War. Four names that are now forgotten. These events lay undiscovered for years having been classified as official secrets. Now published, the files show how the relentless standoff between the two superpowers spiralled out of control and led us to the brink of obliteration. 

 Along with contemporary protagonists, historians, geopolitical specialists and atomic experts, this two-episode documentary takes us first to the Uniteted States, then on European soil, to reveal what we avoided by a whisker during a period that is not really all that far in the past. Returning to this subject casts fresh light on the perils to which the public was exposed at a time of extreme tension, especially as recent historiography will allow us to revisit many shadowy corners of the past, throwing up some completely unexpected answers.

items.content:
<article>From hillbilly to the White House: J. D. Vance’s rise to become Trump’s vice-president is seen by many as symbolic of a worrying trend in the US that’s further polarizing society.

J. D. Vance’s story is the story of an America that has long felt overlooked. An America of the white working class, marked by economic decline, the opioid crisis and the aftermath of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. An America that fears losing even the little that it still holds on to, through migration and social upheaval.
J. D. Vance has undergone a remarkable transformation: from a fierce critic of Donald Trump to a loyal supporter of the MAGA movement and, ultimately, Trump’s vice-president. As far as his supporters are concerned, it is a career trajectory that gives him credibility. Critics, on the other hand, see in his politics a dynamic that could upset the political balance in the US and endanger democracy. Some already regard him as a potential contender for the presidency.

items.title: Hotel hope - Where refugees begin a new life | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>An integration experiment, in the heart of Germany: Refugees move into a vacant hotel, where they receive targeted support. The aim is for them to find work or a training placement, ultimately fostering a successful integration.

An empty hotel in downtown Düsseldorf is ready for a new idea. Karin Jungjohann has one - and isn’t afraid to experiment.

"What do people need most, no matter where they come from? A sense of hope for the future," said Karin Jungjohann, one of the founders of the Düsseldorf language school "Hispi". For years, she had observed how refugees in accommodation centers struggle to progress in their lives. At the same time, she was being approached by restaurateurs in Düsseldorf looking for people to fill jobs in the catering industry. This gave rise to the idea for a project designed to rethink the accommodation, support and integration of refugees: the House of Friends.

A film crew follows the initiator of the integration experiment from the initial selection of participants, through to their successful integration into the labor market and society.

items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Human rights abuses have been reported in the tuna industry, with working conditions described by some as modern slavery. This forced labor has also been linked to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing practices.  

Officially, these fishing boats in the Indian Ocean are fishing for tuna. But sailors say they also illegally catch endangered species. They cut off the fins of sharks to sell them at high prices and dump the live animals back into the ocean. 

NGOs and advocates are pushing for tougher regulations to stop poor working conditions, but enforcing labor laws at sea remains a major challenge.

items.title: The Shuttle Disaster That Almost Grounded NASA's Dreams | Full Episode 1 | Once Upon a Time in Space
items.author: PBS
items.content:
<article>Watch more from this series: https://to.pbs.org/4eO25vC
At the height of the Cold War, the Soviet Union dominates the space race with a series of firsts, until the U.S. lands the first men on the moon in 1969. With the dawn of the Space Shuttle in 1976, the U.S. gains further ground on its rivals. In 1978, Ron McNair, Anna Fisher and Mike Mullane are among the group selected by NASA to fly aboard the Shuttle after the agency encouraged aspiring astronauts of all genders and racial backgrounds to apply. 
 
Growing up under segregation in South Carolina, McNair had few role models for a life in space beyond Lieutenant Uhura of Star Trek. Vietnam veteran Mullane arrives at NASA skeptical that women or civilians could possess “the right stuff.” Emergency physician Fisher is thrust into the spotlight as the first mother in space. Her decision to leave her one-year-old daughter to fly into space intensifies the scrutiny.
 
As pressure mounts on the Shuttle program to meet military and commercial demands, disaster strikes in 1986 when Challenger explodes during launch, killing all seven astronauts. While the remaining U.S. shuttle fleet is grounded, the Soviet Union successfully launches Mir, the most sophisticated space station ever seen, and edges ahead in the space race.

items.title: Assaults in the hospital - When doctors harass their female colleagues | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Women who become doctors choose their profession to heal people. But in hospitals, they often become victims of sexual harassment. This film features case studies from Switzerland.

From obscene jokes by powerful bosses in the operating room to sexual blackmail and assaults during training: in this film, female students, doctors, and surgeons recount what they have had to endure. In an environment still marked by a culture of silence, harassers are rarely punished by their superiors.
Often, victims are reluctant to file a complaint for fear of jeopardizing their careers. Some take the risk and report the incidents to human resources, but these complaints are seldom followed up. Although hospitals claim to have a zero-tolerance policy, harassers rarely experience any negative consequences.
